bt = next(c for c in M["claims"] if (c["a"], c["b"], c["eval"]) == ("B", "raw 2B", "test-clean"))

## Choosing a checkpoint

Each run saves a checkpoint every 500 steps. Every checkpoint is scored on validation, and the best
by strict exact is the **selected checkpoint**, a tie going to the earlier one. Only that one is run
on test, test-clean and BFCL. The rule was fixed before any run.

With `{python} n(splits["validation"])` validation rows, neighbouring checkpoints are usually within
noise of each other, so the pick within a run is itself noisy. That doesn't bias the test numbers,
which are scored once on the checkpoint chosen; it means a claim that rests on the pick names it.

::: {.column-margin}
The rule: [ADR 0006](../decisions/0006-shared-training-setup.html); what it can and can't say:
[ADR 0009](../decisions/0009-selection-stays-methods-compared-on-test-clean.html).
:::

## Paired tests

Two models are compared on the same rows. Most rows both get right or both get wrong; the
**McNemar test** looks only at the rows where exactly one is right. B against its teacher on
test-clean:

| | 2B right | 2B wrong |
|---|---:|---:|
| **B right** | | **`{python} bt["only_a_right"]`** |
| **B wrong** | **`{python} bt["only_b_right"]`** | |

If the two were equally good, those `{python} bt["only_a_right"] + bt["only_b_right"]` rows would
split about evenly. A split of `{python} bt["only_a_right"]` against `{python} bt["only_b_right"]`
is very unlikely by chance.

## Many claims at once

The README and this site make `{python} len(M["claims"])` such claims. Testing many raises the chance
that one looks significant by luck, so every claim's p-value is adjusted with **Holm's method** over
all of them, and a claim is called significant only after the adjustment. The family grows as methods
are added, so an earlier claim's adjusted p-value can only rise.

## Methods tie, then cost decides

Where test-clean can't separate methods, no winner is named; the cheaper is published, and when costs
are within 10% of each other, the simpler pipeline. That is why the headline method is B.

## What a GPU-hour includes

Every method's cost starts at zero on the one RTX 3060 and counts everything it needs: the teacher
answering train once (`{python} f"{teacher['gpu_hours']:.1f}"` GPU-hours, for every method trained
on teacher outputs), C's extra pass scoring the teacher's top 20, D's sampling and the teacher's
grading at every step, and training. Validation scoring is the same for every method and isn't
counted. Each label-free method is also reported at **B's budget**: its best checkpoint within B's
GPU-hours.
